glm_bug_semantics: In generate_key()'s sequential-XOR path for on-disk format versions 8 and 10, the implementation accumulated the initial SHA-256(password || salt) snapshot and every normalized hash/KDF-stage output, including the last stage, then normalized the final chain value and appended it again. Because the final chain value is identical to the already-recorded last-stage snapshot, XOR combines that value with itself and removes the last stage. With exactly one memory-hard KDF and no preceding hash stage, the sole expensive stage disappears and the encryption key reduces to the initial cheap SHA-256 snapshot, so an attacker with the encrypted file can test password guesses offline at SHA-256 speed rather than paying the configured KDF cost. Default configurations are not exploitable because earlier hash/KDF stages remain in the XOR.
grok_bug_semantics: In sequential XOR key derivation (on-disk format_version 8/10, --xor), generate_key in openssl_encrypt/modules/crypt_core.py XORs every stage snapshot in xor_accumulator, then also appends sequential_result = normalize(final chain password). That final value equals the last stage's already-stored snapshot, so the last stage XORs to zero and drops out of the key. With a single KDF and no prior hash stage (non-default), the only expensive stage is the last one; the key collapses to the pre-chain SHA256(password||salt) and advertised Argon2/scrypt cost is bypassed for offline guessing.

glm_bug_semantics: The Git node constructed simple-git with a caller-selected local repository as baseDir and then ran Git operations without overriding command-bearing repository-local configuration. Native git therefore loaded values from that repository's .git/config, including values such as core.sshCommand and core.fsmonitor that cause external programs to run. An attacker who first used a separate file-write vulnerability to plant such a value could make a later Git-node operation execute a command as the n8n process user; the Git node's own addConfig key restrictions did not protect configuration written directly to disk.

Those values were not overridden or neutralized, so any later Git-node operation against a repo containing a planted command-bearing key executed that command as the n8n process user. The node's own addConfig UI/API was later restricted to user.email/user.name/remote.origin.url and is not the exploit path; planting required a separate file-write.

glm_bug_semantics: Scriban enforced TemplateContext.LoopLimit only when script-level for/while loops called StepLoop. A single attacker-controlled expression could instead perform expensive internal iteration without StepLoop: a lazy 1..N range yielded N values and array.size exhausted a non-ICollection with LINQ Count(), while string * int appended in an ordinary for loop. ScriptBlockStatement checked cancellation only once around the whole statement, so these internal loops could consume excessive CPU or memory before another abort check. Applications rendering untrusted templates that treated a small LoopLimit as an execution bound were therefore exposed to denial of service.

glm_bug_semantics: Scriban's recursive-descent expression parser counts nesting in EnterExpression() and, when ExpressionDepthLimit is exceeded, only LogError()s a non-fatal message and sets _isExpressionDepthLimitReached (used solely to dedupe that message). Parsing does not throw, return a sentinel, or unwind. Deeply nested parentheses, array initializers, object initializers, or unary operators therefore keep descending until the native thread stack is exhausted, raising an uncatchable StackOverflowException that kills the host process. Template.Parse, Template.ParseLiquid, and runtime object.eval / object.eval_template share this parser. Versions 6.6.0-7.2.0 ship a default limit of 250 that does not actually halt descent; pre-6.6.0 had the same non-enforcing helper with a null default (unbounded). CWE-674 DoS.

glm_bug_semantics: A local GLX client can send ChangeDrawableAttributes with a request buffer shorter than the numAttribs count claims. Both native and byte-swapped dispatchers compute the required size but compare it in the wrong direction: expected_words < client->req_len. That rejects an overlong request while allowing an undersized one. The native dispatcher then passes req + 1 to DoChangeDrawableAttributes, whose numAttribs loop reads two CARD32 values per claimed attribute beyond the request buffer, disclosing adjacent server memory; the byte-swapped path first swaps the same client-controlled number of words in place, providing an out-of-bounds write path for byte-swapped clients, which the advisory says are disabled by default.
grok_bug_semantics: CWE-125 OOB read in __glXDisp_ChangeDrawableAttributes / __glXDispSwap_ChangeDrawableAttributes: a reversed request-length check compares computed size LESS THAN client->req_len instead of GREATER THAN, so an undersized request whose numAttribs claims more attribute pairs than the buffer contains still passes. DoChangeDrawableAttributes then walks numAttribs pairs from the header and overreads (and can OOB-write eventMask on GLX_EVENT_MASK if a swapped client is enabled).

glm_bug_semantics: Xext/sync.c SyncChangeCounter walks a SyncCounter trigger list by caching pnext = ptl->next, then may invoke pTrigger->TriggerFired. For an XSync Await group that callback is SyncAwaitTriggerFired, which FreeResource()s the Await; FreeAwait then deletes every sibling wait-condition trigger from its SyncObject (SyncDeleteTriggerFromSyncObject, historically SyncDeleteTriggerFromCounter), unlinking and freeing list nodes that can include the cached pnext. The next loop step is therefore a use-after-free (CWE-416). A local client that places multiple Await conditions on counters, then has those counters change (including via a second client), can crash the X server or escalate if it runs as root. glm_bug_semantics: A template-controlled filter name was used as a bracket key on Liquid.filters, a normal JavaScript object. Therefore `valueOf` resolved to the inherited Object.prototype.valueOf even though no such filter had been registered. Filter.render then invoked that inherited function with an engine-owned receiver containing `context`, `liquid`, and, in later versions, `token`; valueOf returned the receiver itself. A crafted template could retain that object, traverse the leaked Liquid engine to its parser/loader/options/filesystem and filter registry, and use the advisory's group_by/where/comparable gadgets to obtain Function and invoke child_process, producing remote code execution. The analogous inherited lookup on Liquid.tags also let names such as `constructor` bypass the unknown-tag check. The fix makes both registries null-prototype objects so inherited Object.prototype members cannot resolve.
grok_bug_semantics: LiquidJS resolved template-controlled filter and tag names with bracket lookup on a prototype-inheriting registry (plain {}). glm_bug_semantics: A local attacker can supply a truncated/malformed IPv6 capture and run tcprewrite with --fixlen pad. tcpedit_packet derives ip6_hdr from the original packet buffer, then untrunc_packet calls realloc through safe_realloc when pkthdr->len exceeds pkthdr->caplen. If realloc moves the allocation, *pktdata is updated but tcpedit_packet's ip6_hdr alias is not. untrunc_packet returns a positive checksum-recalculation signal, so fix_ipv6_checksums later dereferences the freed IPv6-header alias (the reported read is src/tcpedit/edit_packet.c:155 in revision 6fcbf0324088561d95c356fe8337f4faac275f1a), producing a heap use-after-free and crash.

glm_bug_semantics: SQLE used the public constant string "secret" as the HMAC key both to sign JWTs and to authenticate JWTs protecting the /v1 API. Because HS256 verification proves only knowledge of that shared key, a remote attacker who knows the repository-visible constant can create a syntactically valid token with attacker-chosen claims, including an administrative name, and have the middleware accept it. The same default later survived as JWTSecretKey = []byte("secret") in sqle/utils/jwt.go; although a setter was added, current history has no SetSecretKey callsite, so the default remains effective.
grok_bug_semantics: SQLE ships a compile-time JWT HMAC secret of the literal string "secret". The advisory sink is sqle/utils/jwt.go JWTSecretKey (`var JWTSecretKey = []byte("secret")`). glm_bug_semantics: A dependency controls its installed package.json repository and homepage fields. When a user requests repository/homepage columns, npm-check-updates places those strings into a cli-table3 row and prints the row without neutralizing ESC, OSC, CSI, CR, or other terminal control characters. A malicious dependency value therefore reaches the user's terminal and can manipulate terminal-rendered output when ncu is run with the relevant format option.

glm_bug_semantics: Cardboard's public Bukkit World unloadChunk overloads funnel caller-controlled chunk coordinates into unloadChunk0. The vulnerable implementation obtains the NMS WorldChunk, requests an unload, drains queued chunk-manager tasks, and reports the result without first rejecting a chunk that is loaded/in use and without handling a null chunk reference. Thus an unload can be attempted while the chunk is active or unavailable; the first-party fix describes the resulting risk as server crashes, data corruption, and potential remote-code-execution vectors, while the advisory's scored impact is network-reachable high availability impact.

glm_bug_semantics: Bandit's HTTP/2 connection handler appends each received chunk to state.buffer and repeatedly calls Frame.deserialize/2. The oversized-frame clause introduced to enforce max_frame_size destructured not only the 9-byte HTTP/2 header but also _payload::binary-size(length), so an attacker could announce a 24-bit length up to 16,777,215 bytes and keep the parser returning {:more, msg} until that entire body had accumulated. The length > max_frame_size guard therefore ran only after the excessive allocation, allowing unauthenticated h2/h2c peers to amplify per-connection buffering far beyond the negotiated 16 KiB default and cause memory-exhaustion denial of service.
grok_bug_semantics: Bandit.HTTP2.Frame.deserialize/2 in lib/bandit/http2/frame.ex rejected SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE violations only in a clause that also required payload::binary-size(length), so the 24-bit length field was not checked until the entire announced body was already in the connection buffer. Incomplete oversized frames returned {:more, msg} and the HTTP/2 handler kept concatenating bytes. An unauthenticated HTTP/2 peer could announce length=0xFFFFFF (~16 MiB) on a connection that had negotiated the RFC 9113 default 16384-byte max_frame_size and force the server to buffer far beyond the agreed budget (memory-exhaustion DoS / CWE-770). No Plug or application auth is involved; the bug is in the framing layer before any request handling.

This made the newly introduced size check causally too late; the same commit's generic fallback continued to request more bytes for a header whose declared body was not yet complete.

Bandit already rejected comma-separated Content-Length: 0, 43 when values differed, but the multi-line form never reached that check. Combined with HTTP/1 keepalive, leftover body bytes are dispatched as a second pipelined request. Behind a CL-last proxy this is classic CL.CL request smuggling (CWE-444): an unauthenticated client can smuggle a request past edge WAF/ACL/rate-limit/audit that the proxy already applied.

glm_bug_semantics: The in-process TURN server's UDP receive loop is unsupervised and does not isolate datagram processing. ReceiveUdpAsync() wraps only the socket ReceiveAsync in an inner try; HandleUdpDatagram() runs inside the while body but outside any per-datagram handler, and the generic catch (Exception) sits lexically outside the while. A single unauthenticated UDP datagram whose STUN header first byte is 0x80-0xFF makes STUNHeader.ParseSTUNHeader throw ApplicationException; the exception unwinds past the loop, the outer catch logs it and the method returns. Start() launches the loop fire-and-forget (_ = ReceiveUdpAsync()) with no restart logic, so the TURN UDP relay stays dead for every client until process restart — a pre-authentication whole-server denial of service. A second path (too-short datagram with an accepted first byte -> null header -> NullReferenceException in ParseSTUNMessage) exists; the advisory documents the first.

glm_bug_semantics: A negotiated WebRTC peer can send a checksum-valid SCTP SACK chunk whose 16-bit gap-ACK-block and duplicate-TSN counts are inconsistent with its declared chunk length. SctpSackChunk.ParseChunk trusted those attacker-controlled counts as loop bounds and repeatedly called unchecked NetConvert.ParseUInt16/ParseUInt32 beyond the SACK value and eventually beyond the reused 262144-byte receive buffer. The resulting IndexOutOfRangeException bypassed the receive loop's recoverable ApplicationException handler, reached the generic Exception handler, and broke the only SCTP receive thread, permanently denying the association and all data channels.
grok_bug_semantics: SctpSackChunk.ParseChunk reads attacker-controlled numGapAckBlocks and numDuplicateTSNs (each up to 65535) and loops that many times calling NetConvert.ParseUInt16/32 with no check of the counts against the declared chunk length or the 262144-byte reused recvBuffer. A checksum-valid SACK with chunkLength=16 and count 0xFFFF walks past the buffer, raising IndexOutOfRangeException. That SystemException skips RTCSctpTransport.DoReceive catch (ApplicationException) continue and hits catch (Exception) break, so the once-started SCTP receive thread exits with no restart and all data channels die (CWE-125/CWE-755). Below the buffer bound the same loops silently parse leftover bytes as gap/dup reports.

glm_bug_semantics: x0vncserver's live MIT-SHM framebuffer path called shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, size, IPC_CREAT|0777). IPC_PRIVATE selects a new SysV IPC key; it does not override the segment's mode bits. The 0777 mode therefore allowed unrelated local users to attach to the live capture buffer for reading or writing. They could observe screen pixels, alter pixels sent to the VNC client, or corrupt the buffer at a sensitive time and crash x0vncserver. Changing the mode to 0600 restricts attachment to the creating user.

glm_bug_semantics: The kernel's CheckAuth middleware grants RoleAdministrator to any request whose RemoteAddr is loopback for a fixed set of URIs — /assets/, /history/assets/, /export/, /api/system/exit, /api/system/getNetwork, /api/system/getWorkspaceInfo (plus SiYuanAccessAuthCodeBypass when no access-auth code is set). The fixed-port reverse proxy forwards to the kernel over loopback without injecting a token and without trusted-proxy client-IP rewrite, so a forwarded request is seen as 127.0.0.1. glm_bug_semantics: Interpretation conflict between SandboxPolicy's security matcher and the executor's tokenizer (CWE-436): isCommandAllowed() evaluated the RAW command string (quotes preserved) against the blockedCommands/allowedCommands glob lists, while ShellExecutor.execute() ran the identical string through parseCommandLine()/tokenizeCommand(), which STRIP quotes and collapse whitespace before the spawn. A command like "git" status (quoted 'git') fails to match blocklist patterns such as git* on the raw string but tokenizes to the argv [git, status] that the executor runs — and likewise a quoted 'rm -rf /' style payload or an allowed-list command padded with quotes/irregular whitespace can slip past approval gates. The result: blocklist checks and approval gates are evaded while the executor runs the exact unquoted dangerous argv. At v5.15.0 this raw-vs-canonical split is verbatim in lib/agent-runtime.ts (parseCommandLine used only as a metachar gate; matchesAny still fed `trimmed`).

glm_bug_semantics: WEBrick's chunked-body reader ends with `read_header(socket)  # trailer + CRLF` (lib/webrick/httprequest.rb, read_chunked), which unconditionally re-invokes the same header parser used for the initial request head: `@header = HTTPUtils::parse_header(@raw_header.join)` overwrites the canonical request-header hash with the trailer block, then `@header.delete("transfer-encoding")` erases the only record that the request was Transfer-Encoding: chunked. A client can therefore smuggle `Content-Length: N` as a chunked TRAILER: the initial head says `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` (so the CL-vs-TE conflict check in read_body never fires because read_body's self['content-length'] test runs before the trailer reparse), the trailer's Content-Length is parsed straight into @header as canonical request state, and transfer-encoding is then deleted — leaving a request whose canonical state claims both a Content-Length body framing that the server never consumed and no TE marker. Downstream, @remaining_size is reset to 0 while @header['content-length'] survives, so any component that later trusts self['content-length'] (e.g. meta["CONTENT_LENGTH"] in CGI/ERB env setup, or keep-alive pipelining logic) interprets the unread socket bytes as the next request — classic CL-via-trailer request smuggling (CWE-444). The advisory scope is 'through v1.9.2', i.e. every tagged release.

The allowlist itself (basicEnvVars, trustLevel/exposeAllEnv gate) originates in 69dabac27878 / 5fd6361c56e5 (2020-01, Sergio Zharinov) and was functioning correctly before this migration.
